## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vipallāsakathā* ("Discussion of Perversions") is the eighth treatise of the *Mahāvagga* in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, an analytical text of the Pali *Khuddakanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. The work systematically expounds the doctrine of perversions or cognitive distortions (*vipallāsa*), treating the classic categories of distortions of perception (*saññā-vipallāsa*), thought (*citta-vipallāsa*), and view (*diṭṭhi-vipallāsa*) concerning the impermanent (*anicca*), the suffering (*dukkha*), the not-self (*anattā*), and the unattractive or foul (*asubha*) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].

Curated parallels and text-reuse metrics confirm extensive shared material between the *Vipallāsakathā* and other canonical and para-canonical works. SuttaCentral notes its close doctrinal relationship to the *Vipallāsasutta* of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 4.49), the *Peṭakopadesa* (*Suttatthasamuccayabhūmi*, Pe 6), and the *Nettippakaraṇa* (*Samāropanahāravibhaṅga*, Ne 19) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus strongly confirms these connections, recording near-verbatim text reuse between Ps 1.8 (§1.2–7.4) and AN 4.49 (§49.1.1–49.7.4) spanning over 3,200 characters with a 0.99 similarity score [DharmaNexus]. Substantial shared passages also occur with the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 6 and Pe 8), the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 12.9), the *Vibhaṅga* (Vb 17), the *Visuddhimagga*, and the *Nettippakaraṇa* along with its commentary and subcommentary [DharmaNexus]. Beyond the Pali tradition, DharmaNexus aligns passages of Ps 1.8 with Tibetan texts—notably the *Abhidharmakośaṭīkā* (D4092-2) and the *Vyaktapadāsuhṛllekhaṭīkā* (D4190)—and the Chinese *Daji famen jing* (大集法門經, T 12) [DharmaNexus].

While modern scholars widely discuss the four *vipallāsa* in connection with early discourse collections, mindfulness practice, and psychological frameworks, secondary literature in the research dossier discusses the *Aṅguttaranikāya* discourse or the general doctrinal concept rather than focusing on Ps 1.8 itself.
